prompt: An ISP sells 900 Mbit/s plans to 32 homes sharing one XGS-PON with about 10 Gbit/s downstream. Customers usually get close to 900 Mbit/s in speed tests. What explains this, and when would they notice the sharing?

options.text: Fibre is not shared, so each home always has its own 10 Gbit/s
options.explanation: A PON's downstream is a shared stream split passively among homes. The 10 Gbit/s is the total for the whole split.

options.text: Homes rarely all download at full speed at once, so one busy home can get near its plan rate; if all 32 demanded it simultaneously, they would share about 10 Gbit/s, roughly 300 Mbit/s each with equal sharing
options.explanation: Correct. Together the plans add up to nearly three times the PON's capacity, which works because demand peaks rarely coincide. Real scheduling, overhead and other bottlenecks change the exact share.

options.text: The ISP must be selling only 900 Mbit/s in total across all 32 homes
options.explanation: Plans are sold per home. The point is that their total exceeds the shared capacity, relying on statistical multiplexing.

options.text: Each home gets a fixed 1/32 of the capacity, about 300 Mbit/s, all the time
options.explanation: Shares are not permanently reserved: an idle neighbour's capacity is available to others, which is why speed tests usually reach the plan rate.

workedExample:
1. A PON shares one downstream optical channel among all homes on the split, about 10 Gbit/s for XGS-PON before overhead.
2. 32 plans of 900 Mbit/s add up to 28.8 Gbit/s, nearly three times that capacity: the access network is oversubscribed by design.
3. This works because homes rarely all download flat out at once. A single busy home can get close to its plan rate while others are quiet.
4. In the rare moment when everyone demands their full rate, they share the PON: with equal sharing and no other bottleneck, about 300 Mbit/s each.
5. Real line rates, protocol overhead, scheduler policy and the ISP's aggregation and transit capacity all affect what customers actually see.

prompt: You are planning connectivity for an island nation served by two submarine cables that land on the same stretch of coast. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fishing and anchoring are major documented causes of cable faults, especially where human activity overlaps cable routes
options.explanation: Correct. ICPC’s June 2025 summary attributes 70–80% of recorded faults to accidental damage, primarily fishing and vessel anchoring; other causes also exist.

options.text: Marine repair can be prolonged by ship availability, weather, permits and the work of recovering and splicing cable
options.explanation: Correct. Exact duration and method depend on the fault and system; there is no universal repair deadline.

options.text: Satellites carry most intercontinental traffic, so a cable cut barely matters
options.explanation: Submarine cables are central to intercontinental connectivity. Satellite backup may help, but its available capacity and terminals must be planned rather than assumed sufficient.

options.text: In long-haul repeatered systems, optical amplifiers can receive power from shore-fed high-voltage DC
options.explanation: Correct. Repeater spacing, voltage and design vary, and unrepeatered cable systems also exist.

options.text: With two cables, any single event leaves the country fully connected
options.explanation: Two cables landing in the same place can be cut by one earthquake, landslide or dragged anchor. And even if one survives, it may lack the capacity for all the rerouted traffic.

workedExample: The supported claims concern documented damage mechanisms, repair logistics and shore-fed power in repeatered systems. Two cables sharing a landing area can share physical hazards or terrestrial backhaul. Resilience improves through route/landing diversity and adequate surviving capacity; backup satellites are not an automatic full-capacity substitute.
